title: I cross lances with horsemen. Time rides in their ranks
intro: Al-Mutanabbi addresses Ali ibn Ahmad ibn Amir of Antioch, himself a poet and a generous host. Before naming him, the visitor describes his quarrel with Time and takes us across a waste where the ground itself seems to travel. Rain leads him to his host’s family, and by the end one man has given him reason to forgive the world.

translation: I cross lances with horsemen. Time rides in their ranks,
and I ride alone. Why say that, with patience beside me?
1.sharh: Calamities take the shape of cavalry, with Time riding among them. The speaker hears himself say “alone” and corrects the word before the line is over.

translation: Braver than I, day after day, is my safety.
It holds its ground with something in mind.
2.sharh: Safety itself has shown extraordinary nerve by staying with such a reckless man. Its persistence makes him suspect it has plans of its own.

translation: I grappled with disasters until I left them asking,
“Has death died? Has terror taken fright?”
3.sharh: Disasters, usually the cause of fear, have become the bewildered speakers. Each of their two questions turns an affliction back upon itself.

translation: I charged like a torrent, as though I had
another life, or a blood debt against my own.
4.sharh: A flash flood supplies the force of the charge. He treats the one life he has as something either replaceable or deserving of revenge.

translation: Let the soul take its fill before it goes.
Two neighbours must part whose home is a lifetime.
5.sharh: Body and soul are neighbours with a common lease. Its expiry gives urgency to the appeal to let the soul exercise its powers.

translation: Never mistake a wineskin and a singing girl for glory.
Glory is the sword and the unprecedented stroke,
6.sharh: The wineskin and singer stand for a life spent enjoying wealth. His competing definition of glory begins here and runs through the next two verses.

translation: striking kings again and again on neck and crown,
the black dust clouds yours, the vast army yours,
7.sharh: The repeated blows fall on the highest heads in the land. The view then widens from the individual blow to the whole army and the dust it raises.

translation: leaving such a roar in the world
as ten fingertips taking turns at a man’s ears.
8.sharh: The comparison asks the listener to try an experiment. Press and release a finger at the ear and a roar comes from within, however quiet the world outside.

translation: If your worth cannot spare you thanking a lesser man
for a gift, the honour goes to the one you thank.
9.sharh: A gift can reverse the order of merit by making its recipient indebted. Al-Wahidi takes “the one who has the thanks” to mean the inferior man publicly honoured by them.

translation: Whoever spends his hours amassing wealth
for fear of poverty makes himself poor.
10.sharh: Time is what the hoarder actually spends. Living without the use of his possessions gives him precisely the impoverished life he is saving to avoid.

translation: Against the unjust I pledge every bounding mare,
a young rider on her back, his chest full of rancour.
11.sharh: The opening is the language of a pledge. The mare brings physical energy, while the feeling filling her rider’s chest gives the charge its motive.

translation: With his spearpoints he passes round among them
cups of death where no one cares for wine.
12.sharh: The rider makes the rounds like a cupbearer. The pleasure of the drinking party earlier in the poem has given way to an utterly unwanted draught.

translation: I crossed mountains that testify I am
the mountains, and seas that swear I am the sea.
13.sharh: The landscape he has travelled can testify to what he is made of. Mountain steadfastness and oceanic bounty are recognised by their natural counterparts.

translation: In many a waste our camels rode the desert’s back
as we rode theirs, sitting mid-saddle.
14.sharh: Imagine three layers, riders on camels on the immense back of the waste. From the riders’ height the camels’ backs become the saddle of the desert itself.

translation: They stride with us through its heart as if we rode
on a ball, or the land too were travelling with us.
15.sharh: Featureless ground gives no measure of progress. A turning ball and a landscape travelling at the camels’ pace are his two explanations for the sensation.

translation: Many a day we ran into a night
whose horizon wore red robes woven out of lightning,
16.sharh: The caravan goes straight from day into night. Lightning gives the edge of that night the sudden colour and folds of red robes.

translation: and many a night into a day
whose back wore dark green robes of cloud.
17.sharh: Daybreak brings no clearing. The green of these cloud-robes shades towards black in older Arabic, a countercolour to the lightning-red of the night.

translation: Under one downpour we thought Amir
had risen alive, or had his grave in the clouds,
18.sharh: The downpour introduces the patron’s grandfather. Either he has gone up alive to give from the clouds, or the very place of his burial has caught his generosity.

translation: or his surviving grandson Ali ibn Ahmad
bestowed this rain, except that I came through empty-handed.
19.sharh: Another possible source of the rain is Ali himself. The empty hand is the traveller’s witty objection to his own fancy, since no one leaves Ali without a personal gift.

translation: A cloud whose downpour rivalled his giving
could boast of it over every cloud in the sky.
20.sharh: The two Arabic words sound almost alike, one for heavy rain and one for generosity. It is the cloud that gains prestige from the comparison.

translation: No heart could contain his heart’s ambitions.
If one held them, no chest could hold that heart.
21.sharh: Ambition is given a physical volume. Each imaginary container proves too small, first the heart, then even the chest that would have to house it.

translation: His means would help no one without his generosity.
What use are brown spears without hands to wield them?
22.sharh: Means alone do nothing for a person in need. The spear lying idle makes the gap between a resource and the will to use it visible.

translation: Al-Salt and Amir came together in one conjunction,
as an Indian blade and victory come together.
23.sharh: The maternal and paternal lines converge like stars in conjunction. An Indian steel sword paired with victory supplies a second likeness for their union.

translation: They brought forth a man of shining brow, held in honour.
The crowd around him seems a mere handful.
24.sharh: The adjective for his clear brow echoes the name of his grandfather al-Salt. Sheer presence makes the large crowd around him count for little.

translation: Men would ransom that great lord with their fathers.
His generosity is a tide that never ebbs.
25.sharh: The formula of devotion stakes the most precious kin a man can name. The sea supplies a further extravagance, a tide from which ebb has been removed.

translation: Longing kept leading me towards him.
His name rode beside me in every caravan.
26.sharh: There is a second travelling companion beside the longing that guides him. Wherever he joins a caravan, talk of Ali is already there.

translation: Before we met I thought the reports tremendous.
When we met, experience made the reports seem small.
27.sharh: A single vowel separates the Arabic for a report from knowledge gained at first hand. Meeting Ali changes the apparent size of everything the poet had heard.

translation: We thrust towards you across each level reach
on stout camels. All they met was an exposed throat.
28.sharh: He borrows the verb of a spear-thrust for travel. The flat country offers no more resistance to the camels than a bare throat to the point.

translation: If a sting raised a swelling she frisked at it,
as though a gadfly had tied a gift into her hide.
29.sharh: The camel’s movement from pain is provocatively read as a dance of delight. The little lump under the skin has the shape of a purse tied around a gift.

translation: We reached you. The sun and moon lay farther off.
In all your qualities the sun and moon fall short of you.
30.sharh: The first comparison measures how far the travellers had to go. The second measures worth, and the sun and moon now occupy the lower place.

translation: You are the coolness of water. There is no life without it.
Were you that water, camels would never wait ten days to drink.
31.sharh: Camels in dry country could go on a long watering cycle. Water endowed with Ali’s generosity would be available too freely for that interval to be needed.

translation: Knowledge, forbearance and judgement called me to you,
as did your words in verse and the gifts you scatter.
32.sharh: Arabic sets arranging beside scattering, the verbs behind verse-making and lavish gifts. Ali is a poet as well as the patron of the man speaking.

translation: My own verse called me too. Its lines shine so brightly
that the ink almost turns white when they are written.
33.sharh: His own praise of Ali was another reason for the journey. He imagines its light passing into the very ink people use to copy it.

translation: The meanings shining through their eloquence seem
the Pleiades, or your own radiant qualities.
34.sharh: The tight cluster of the Pleiades gives the meanings a visible arrangement. The second likeness turns from the heavens to the character that produced the lines.

translation: Hatred of rulers kept me from their company,
as did the vulture demanding their skulls of me.
35.sharh: He accounts for his usual distance from rulers with a grisly piece of fantasy. The scavenger treats him as a debtor who owes it the heads of kings.

translation: I found hardship a better sight,
and easier to bear than a small man swollen with pride.
36.sharh: The humiliation of attending an inferior man can cost more than material hardship. Smallness and self-importance jostle in a single phrase.

translation: My tongue, my eye, my heart and my ambition
are friends to their namesakes in you, their other half.
37.sharh: Each part of the poet has a friend of the same name in Ali. We follow Ibn Jinni’s image of the two as halves of one whole. Another commentator sees a debt of education and standing.

translation: I did not speak all this poetry on my own.
My verse about you has poetry of its own.
38.sharh: The poem joins the company of those eager to praise Ali. For a moment the poet has a collaborator, his own verse speaking on its own account.

translation: The beauty you see in it is no mere polish.
Its face lit up when it turned to you.
39.sharh: The poem now has a face. Its glow is the flush of pleasure at seeing Ali, an expression more intimate than a polished surface.

translation: Even if you reached the sky, I would know
you had yet to reach what your worth deserves.
40.sharh: The conditional grants Ali the highest position imaginable. Even after that concession, the poet says there is still a disparity between rank and merit.

translation: Through you the days have put my grievance to rest.
Their children are their offence, and you their excuse.
41.sharh: Time, the enemy rider in the opening, can at last make peace. Its other children are the charge against it, and Ali alone supplies its defence.

1.1.1.head: طاعَنَ
1.1.1.meaning: To exchange lance-thrusts with an opponent.

1.1.2.head: خَيل
1.1.2.meaning: Mounted troops, here the army of misfortunes.

2.1.5.head: سَلامَة
2.1.5.meaning: His immunity from harm, imagined as a companion that stands its ground.

3.1.1.head: تَمَرَّسَ
3.1.1.meaning: To grapple repeatedly with something and know its force.

3.2.5.meaning: To be terrified, here said of terror itself.

4.1.3.head: الأَتِيّ
4.1.3.meaning: A torrent that comes down from rain falling elsewhere.

4.2.7.head: وِتر
4.2.7.meaning: A blood debt or grievance calling for vengeance.

5.1.6.head: بَين
5.1.6.meaning: Separation, here the parting of soul and body.

6.1.4.head: زِقّ
6.1.4.meaning: A skin used to hold wine or other liquids.

6.1.5.head: قَينَة
6.1.5.meaning: A singing slave girl at a drinking party.

6.2.5-6.head: الفَتكَة البِكر
6.2.5-6.meaning: “A maiden stroke”: a surprise attack without precedent.

7.1.2-4.head: أَعناق المُلوك وَهامُها
7.1.2-4.meaning: “The necks and crowns of kings.” Al-Wahidi’s text reads “men’s necks, and that you see”. The reciter names the kings and their heads.

7.2.2.head: هَبوَة
7.2.2.meaning: A cloud of dust rising from the ground.

7.2.5.head: مَجر
7.2.5.meaning: Vast in number, particularly of an army.

9.1.7.head: ناقِص
9.1.7.meaning: A man deficient in merit or generosity of spirit.

11.1.5.head: طِمِرَّة
11.1.5.meaning: A spirited mare that bounds forward.

11.2.5.head: غِمر
11.2.5.meaning: A grudge held deep in the heart.

12.2.1-2.head: كُؤوس المَنايا
12.2.1-2.meaning: “Cups of death”: death handed round like wine.

13.1.4.head: جابَ
13.1.4.meaning: To traverse a tract of country.

14.1.3.head: العيس
14.1.3.meaning: Pale camels, here the caravan’s riding animals.

14.2.4-5.head: واسِط الكور
14.2.4-5.meaning: “The middle of the camel saddle”: its supporting central piece.

15.1.1.head: وَخَدَ
15.1.1.meaning: To travel with the long quick stride of a camel.

15.1.4.head: جَوز
15.1.4.meaning: The middle or heart of a region.

15.2.6.head: سَفر
15.2.6.meaning: A company of travellers. The ground is imagined joining it.

17.2.4.head: دَجن
17.2.4.meaning: A dark overcast. The consonant in the recording sounds close to z. The commentaries give dajn, cloud-darkness.

18.1.5.head: عامِر
18.1.5.meaning: Amir, Ali’s paternal grandfather, recalled for his generosity.

19.2.7.head: صِفر
19.2.7.meaning: Empty, here of a hand carrying no gift.

20.1.3.head: جَود
20.1.3.meaning: A copious downpour, close in sound to the word for generosity.

21.1.5.head: هِمَّة
21.1.5.meaning: A high aim a person is resolved to reach.

22.1.3.head: الإِمكان
22.1.3.meaning: Means or resources at one’s disposal.

23.1.1.head: قِران
23.1.1.meaning: A conjunction of two heavenly bodies, applied to two family lines.

23.2.3.head: الهِندُوانِيّ
23.2.3.meaning: Hinduwani, a blade of the prized Indian steel.

24.1.3-4.head: صَلت الجَبين
24.1.3-4.meaning: “Clear-browed”: also an echo of the grandfather’s name.

24.2.3.head: قُلّ
24.2.3.meaning: Few or of little account, used collectively.

25.1.4.head: سَمَيذَع
25.1.4.meaning: A noble and generous lord. The commentaries on the poem spell the word with d. Ibn al-Hanbali also records the dh pronounced here.

27.2.4-5.head: الخَبَر وَالخُبر
27.2.4-5.meaning: “Report” and “experience”, distinguished in Arabic by one vowel.

28.1.6.head: صَفصَف
28.1.6.meaning: A flat, even expanse of ground.

29.2.3.meaning: To tie something up in a small purse or bundle.

29.2.6.head: نِبر
29.2.6.meaning: A fly whose sting raises a lump on a camel’s hide.

31.2.7.head: العِشر
31.2.7.meaning: The long watering cycle on which camels drink on the tenth day.

32.2.4-5.head: النّائِل النَّثر
32.2.4-5.meaning: “Scattered gifts”, paired with the careful arranging of words into verse.

33.1.2.head: قالَ
33.1.2.meaning: “I spoke.” Al-Mutanabbi means his own verse. The Berlin edition of al-Wahidi reads “you spoke”, making the verse Ali’s. Mu'jiz Ahmad records both readings.

34.2.2.meaning: The Pleiades, a bright, close cluster of stars.

35.2.2.head: اِقتَضى
35.2.2.meaning: To demand repayment of a debt.

37.2.1.head: أَوُدّ
37.2.1.meaning: Friends or intimates, an uncommon plural in Ibn Jinni’s reading.

37.2.6.head: شَطر
37.2.6.meaning: A half, here each person’s counterpart in the other.

39.2.6.head: بِشر
39.2.6.meaning: The brightness of a welcoming face.

40.1.2.head: إِن
40.1.2.meaning: “Even if” in the recording. The two commentaries print the equivalent construction with law.

41.1.4.head: عَتب
41.1.4.meaning: A grievance or reproach directed at someone from whom one expects better.
